title: Facility for drunks, addicts needed here
article: Calgary's police chief and the head of the police commission both want to get drunks and addicts out of city cells and into treatment.
"This is something we're really keen on doing," says Dave Mitchell, chairman of the commission. "We've been working on it for quite a while.
"It's often not appropriate for people who are intoxicated to be in jail cells. We'd like to move them into facilities where they can get care and treatment.
"This is obviously the right thing for the police service, but it's the best thing for those people too."
Police chief Jack Beaton agrees that drunks and addicts shouldn't stay in police custody unless there's serious criminal activity as well.
"I'm talking about the addicts," he says. "When it comes to traffickers, I don't have much sympathy."
Some experts, including Dermot Baldwin of the Calgary Drop In Centre, say the city needs a stand-alone facility to deal with severely intoxicated people.
"The problem is money," he says. "This is a provincial matter and the money isn't there."
Three men have died in city drunk tanks since 1988. Last week, an addict, Tamer Sayed Roha, died after he was arrested by police at a motel.
Police say Roha was wild and violent, but his grieving family, which had tried to get him into treatment, still wants answers.
Whatever the facts of that case, the sad truth is that addicts and alcoholics are flooding the police service.
"About 17 per cent of the stays in city custody are intoxicated people," says Mitchell. "That's far too many."
People in cells often can't be watched full time, and staff aren't the best people to deal with a sudden medical crisis.
"The police take the tough ones," says Baldwin, the Drop In Centre's executive director.

"Some are prone to extreme violence. The police are equipped for them in a security sense, but, in a rehabilitation sense, it would be better if we had the resources to do it, or some other agency that has an interest."
Those downtown agencies, meanwhile, are also struggling to house and help an exploding population of substance abusers.
The Calgary Drop In Centre alone takes in about 160 to 180 a day at this time of year. The annual total is more than 50,000 visits.
Many are dropped off by police officers because the cases aren't considered overly serious.
But police often have to return later and haul the same people off to the cells.
Baldwin says the influx of addicts and drunks place an incredible strain on the other residents.
"When you mix drugs and alcohol, people hardened in the drug scene, along with people with mental health problems, and others who are bankrupt or homeless, obviously it's difficult.
"We're not a hospital, we're not a clinic, we're not a police department, although in some ways we've become all those things.
"We do well with what we have, but we're bursting at the seams."
The Drop In Centre has been negotiating with the police service for two years, trying to figure out how to take the harder cases while expanding capacity to deal with less serious ones.
For Baldwin, the answer is always the same -- a new centre where substance abusers can get medical help when they're in crisis, and proper counselling and treatment afterward.
Dave Mitchell, meanwhile, is determined to find a solution that keeps these people out of the jail cells.
"Six months to a year, that's my hope," he says. "It has to be done."
